# Pañcattaya Sutta (MN 102 (PTS MN ii 228))
**ID:** MN 102 (PTS MN ii 228)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Pañcattaya Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Five and Three
**PTS:** MN ii 228
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn102
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pañcattaya Sutta* ("The Five and Three", MN 102; PTS MN ii 228) is a discourse in the Majjhimanikāya that functions as a middle-length counterpart to the *Brahmajāla Sutta* (DN 1), systematically surveying and dismissing an array of speculative views [SuttaCentral]. The text analyzes diverse metaphysical doctrines formulated by recluses and brahmans concerning the post-mortem survival and condition of the self—whether after death the self is percipient, non-percipient, or neither; whether it has form, is formless, or both; and whether it perceives unity, diversity, the limited, or the immeasurable [Polak 2011; Radich 2007]. It also investigates cosmological and pre-existent speculations, such as the thesis that the soul and world were completely happy (*ekanta-sukhī attā ca loko ca*), enumerating sixteen positions accepted on subjective grounds such as faith (*saddhā*) or rational reflection (*diṭṭhi-nijjhāna-kkhanti*) [Jayatilleke 1963]. Declaring all these speculative doctrines to be "conditioned and gross" (*saṅkhata* and *oḷārika*), the Buddha rejects them in favor of liberation detached from conceptual proliferation and rarified modes of perception [Jayatilleke 1963; Stuart 2012; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Radich 2007].
Curated parallels listed on SuttaCentral include Sanskrit fragments (SHT sutta 24; SF 57) and a translation in the Tibetan Kangyur (D 294, *mDo chen po lṅa gsum pa*) [SuttaCentral; Fagernes 1992; Stuart 2012]. Automatically computed text-reuse matches from DharmaNexus strongly corroborate the doctrinal closeness between MN 102 and the *Brahmajāla Sutta* (DN 1), sharing over 29,000 characters across 472 matching segments, while also identifying significant textual overlaps with the *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), and *Pāsādika Sutta* (DN 29) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments by DharmaNexus also highlight shared passages with the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi*, Chinese *Dīrghāgama* texts (T 1 and T 25), and Tibetan versions of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* (D 352) [DharmaNexus].
